The usual shorthand, that zero was invented in India, is not so much false as compressed: it squeezes a process into a point, and hides the question that matters, which is what, exactly, was invented.

At least three things travel under the name. The first is zero as a placeholder: a mark showing that a position in a numeral is empty, so that 205 can be told from 25. The Babylonians, who wrote numbers in base sixty, were using a sign for this purpose, two slanted wedges, by about 300 BCE, and the Maya independently developed a shell-shaped glyph for an empty place. The second is zero as a quantity, the answer to the question "how many are left?" when everything has been taken away. The third, and the most demanding, is zero as a number: an object in its own right, which can be added, subtracted and multiplied, and whose properties must be stated. The Babylonians had the first of these but there is little evidence that they had the third. Their placeholder was often left out at the end of a numeral, where it would have changed the magnitude, so that a reader had to consult the context to know whether a figure meant one or sixty.

A number, for them, was a collection of units, and a collection of no units was not a collection. Aristotle, moreover, argued against the existence of a void, holding a vacuum to be a contradiction in terms, and this position made it harder to treat nothing as an object of study. It would be too neat to say that philosophy prevented the Greeks from discovering zero; their astronomers used a positional system borrowed from Babylon, with a symbol for the empty place. The chart measured registrations, not donations. A person registered as a donor is not thereby a donor: organs can be used only if death occurs in circumstances, usually in an intensive-care unit, that make removal possible, and only if the hospital is able to carry out the procedure. Intensive-care beds, surgical teams and the capacity to match organs to recipients are all links in the chain, and the chain is only as strong as its weakest. In practice the family is almost always consulted, and in many countries relatives can and do refuse even where the deceased had registered consent. Rates of actual donation per million inhabitants correlate only loosely with the legal default. Spain, which has consistently had one of the highest rates in the world, has had presumed consent in law since 1979, but its donation rate was unremarkable for a decade afterwards; it rose steeply only after 1989, when the country created a national transplant organisation and placed trained coordinators in hospitals, whose task is to identify potential donors and to approach their families with skill and sympathy. The law did not change at that point. The organisation of the system did.

Studies of countries that changed their defaults tell a similar story. Some have seen donation rates rise modestly; others have seen little change, and a few have seen a fall, perhaps because the change provoked a backlash among people who felt that the state was claiming ownership of their bodies. Wales, which introduced a system of deemed consent in 2015, saw consent rates rise among eligible donors, but the effect on the number of transplants has been hard to disentangle from other reforms made at the same time. The sceptics' conclusion is not that defaults are irrelevant, but that their effect is conditional: it depends on how the default interacts with the rest of the system, including the willingness of families to agree and the capacity of hospitals to act.

Policy designers have also experimented with variants that sit between the two defaults. Under mandated choice, citizens must state a preference when they renew a driving licence or an identity card, so that no default operates at all. Under a soft opt-out, families are consulted and can override the presumption, while a hard system treats it as binding. Each variant trades the same values off differently: mandated choice respects active consent but may leave many with no recorded preference, soft systems protect families but reproduce the problem of refusals, and hard systems maximise supply at the greatest cost to public trust. No arrangement escapes the trade-off; it can only be placed.

There is also a question that the behavioural argument leaves aside: whether silence should count as consent at all. Consent in medicine is meant to be informed and active; a signature on a form is a person's own act, whereas a failure to opt out may reflect ignorance of the law or simply inertia. Defenders of presumed consent answer that no organ is removed without the question being put to relatives, and that the real choice, between a system that wastes organs and one that saves lives, is a moral one in which a modest cost to autonomy is outweighed by lives saved. Critics reply that the moral argument cannot rest on a procedural trick, and that a system which depends on people not noticing how consent is being inferred from them is hard to reconcile with the trust on which donation itself depends.

The lesson is not to abandon defaults but to be modest about them. A default is a lever, not a mechanism: it moves a system only when the parts to which it is attached are able to move. Countries that want more transplants will do better by training coordinators, building intensive-care capacity and talking to families than by relying on a change in the statute, however elegant the chart that recommends it.
questions.question: The critics of presumed consent mentioned in the passage would most likely agree that
options: A) presumed consent is morally wrong in every case, because consent in medicine must always be given in writing.
B) inferring consent from silence may undermine the trust on which donation itself depends.
C) families should be denied any role in decisions about donation, since their refusals waste organs that could save lives.
D) the defenders of presumed consent have no answer to the objection that silence cannot be consent in any circumstances.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The critics say a system that depends on people not noticing how consent is inferred is 'hard to reconcile with the trust on which donation itself depends'. B, C and D overstate or invent positions.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: Millions of birds die each year after striking glass buildings. Is it just bad luck?

Ecologist: Not at all. Birds cannot perceive glass as a barrier. They see the reflection of sky or trees, or they see through to a plant on the other side, and they fly at it. At night the problem is lights: migrating birds are drawn to bright cities, circle, tire and collide. So we have two different problems, with different remedies.

Interviewer: What works?

Ecologist: For daytime strikes, anything that makes the glass visible: patterns of dots or lines spaced closely enough, because birds will not fly through gaps they judge too small. A single hawk silhouette sticker is mostly useless, which surprises people, because a bird can fly past it to the clear glass beside it. For the night, switching off lights during migration seasons has been shown to cut collisions sharply, and it saves energy too.
questions.question: According to the ecologist, daytime collisions occur chiefly because
options: A) migrating birds are attracted to bright lights, circle the buildings, become exhausted and then collide with the walls.
B) birds are unable to see the patterns of dots or lines that building owners have placed on their windows.
C) glass buildings reflect so much sunlight that birds are blinded for several seconds as they pass them.
D) birds cannot perceive glass as a barrier, mistaking reflections or the view through it for open space.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says birds see reflections of sky or trees, or see through to a plant, and fly at it. B describes the night problem; C and D are not claimed.

questions.question: The ecologist's remark about the hawk silhouette sticker suggests that
options: A) birds are frightened of predators, and so will avoid any glass that carries an image of one.
B) a deterrent works only if it makes the whole pane visible, and not merely a part of it.
C) stickers are better than patterns of dots because they cost less to produce and to install.
D) no remedy for daytime strikes has yet been shown to work in any building anywhere.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A single sticker fails because the bird 'can fly past it to the clear glass beside it', whereas closely spaced patterns work. B contradicts his statement; C is not mentioned; D contradicts his account of what works.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. With such a clock, a navigator could compare local noon with the reference time and calculate how far east or west the ship had travelled.
2. For centuries, sailors could find their latitude by the sun, but not their longitude.
3. In the eighteenth century, John Harrison built a marine chronometer that kept accurate time through months of rolling seas.
4. The difficulty was that determining longitude required knowing the exact time at a fixed reference point while at sea.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the old problem (latitude but not longitude). 4 explains the difficulty (exact reference time). 3 ('In the eighteenth century') brings Harrison's chronometer, and 1 ('With such a clock') shows how it was used. Order: 2-4-3-1.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Augustin Fresnel then devised a lens of concentric glass rings that gathered the light and projected it as a narrow beam far out to sea.
2. The result was a light that could be seen from many kilometres away using far less fuel than before.
3. Early lighthouses burned wood or coal on open platforms, and their flames were easily obscured by wind and rain.
4. In the late eighteenth century, the Argand lamp, with its hollow wick, produced a brighter and steadier flame.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 describes the early lighthouses. 4 ('In the late eighteenth century') gives the first improvement. 1 ('then') adds Fresnel's lens, and 2 ('The result') states the outcome of the two improvements. Order: 3-4-1-2.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The fear can therefore fulfil itself, bringing down a bank that was sound when the panic started.
2. A bank run begins when depositors fear that a bank cannot repay them.
3. Because banks lend out most of what they take in, they cannot repay everyone at once, so each depositor's fear is justified if enough others share it.
4. Deposit insurance was designed to break this cycle by assuring depositors that their money is safe whatever others do.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 introduces the run. 3 explains why the fear can be justified. 1 ('therefore') draws the self-fulfilling conclusion, and 4 ('this cycle') presents the remedy. Order: 2-3-1-4.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Within a few generations, Byzantine workshops were producing silk of their own.
2. According to tradition, the secret escaped in the sixth century, when monks carried silkworm eggs hidden in hollow canes to Constantinople.
3. As a result, the monopoly that had lasted for many centuries was broken, and the price of silk in the West fell.
4. Silk was once so valuable that its method of manufacture was a closely guarded secret in China.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states the secret. 2 ('the secret escaped') tells how it escaped. 1 ('Within a few generations') gives the local development, and 3 ('As a result') draws the final consequence. Order: 4-2-1-3.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Economists distinguish between the price of a good and its cost. The price is what the buyer pays; the cost includes whatever else is given up, such as time, convenience and the next-best use of the money. A free concert, therefore, is not free to the person who spends two hours queuing for it, and a cheap flight that lands at a distant airport may be dearer than an expensive one that does not. Decisions based on price alone are thus often mistaken for decisions based on cost.'
options: A) Cost is wider than price, since it includes what is given up, so choices that look cheap may not be.
B) Free goods do not exist, and so the government should never provide concerts or other events to citizens without a charge.
C) Cheap flights are always more expensive than costly ones, because they land at airports that are far from city centres.
D) Economists regard price as irrelevant to decisions, since only the time spent in obtaining a good matters in practice.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph distinguishes price from the wider notion of cost and warns against deciding on price alone. The others overgeneralise ('never', 'always', 'irrelevant').

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Many ancient cities were built beside rivers, and it is easy to attribute this to water for drinking and farming. Rivers, however, also served as highways in an age without good roads, carrying grain, timber and stone at a fraction of the cost of carrying them overland. A city on a river could feed a large population from a wide hinterland, and its merchants could reach distant markets. Control of the river was often the foundation of a city's power.'
options: A) Ancient cities were built beside rivers solely because the water was needed for drinking and for the irrigation of crops in the fields.
B) Roads were unknown in ancient times, and so no city that was far from a river could grow to any considerable size or influence.
C) Merchants in river cities were the most powerful class, and they alone decided where new cities were to be built in the region.
D) Cities grew beside rivers not only for water but because rivers were cheap highways for trade and supply, which gave them power.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph adds transport and trade to the usual water explanation. B contradicts 'however'; C and D overstate or invent claims.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The word "average" suggests a typical case, but an average can describe no one at all. If a town's households have an average of 2.4 children, no household has 2.4 children. When a distribution is lopsided, the mean may be far from the experience of most people: a few very large incomes can raise a town's average income while the majority earn less. For this reason statisticians often prefer the median, the middle value, which is not distorted by extreme cases.'
options: A) Averages are meaningless, and statisticians have therefore abandoned them in favour of the median in all of their work.
B) A town's average income is raised by its poorest households, who are the most numerous within the town.
C) An average can misrepresent a lopsided distribution, so the median is often a better guide to what is typical.
D) No household in any town can have an average number of children, and so surveys of families are unreliable.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph says averages can mislead when data are lopsided and that the median is often preferred. B overstates ('abandoned', 'all'); C reverses the effect of very large incomes; D draws an unrelated conclusion about surveys.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A colony of ants has no leader: no ant knows the plan of the nest or directs the work. ________ Each ant follows simple rules, such as turning towards a stronger trail of scent, and the colony's elaborate behaviour emerges from the interaction of thousands of such acts. The intelligence, if the word is apt, lies in the system and not in any member of it.'
options: A) Yet the colony finds food, builds nests and defends itself with remarkable efficiency.
B) The queen, which issues commands to the workers, is therefore the cleverest member of the colony.
C) Ants are the only insects whose behaviour can be explained without reference to the individual.
D) Colonies are therefore less successful than animals that are organised under a single leader.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The blank must set up the paradox that a leaderless colony behaves in an organised way, which the next sentences explain. B contradicts 'no leader'; C and D introduce claims the paragraph does not make.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'It is often assumed that more information produces better decisions. ________ A manager given a hundred pages of data may attend to the most vivid detail rather than the most relevant, and decide worse than one given a single page. When attention is scarce, the cost of information is the attention it consumes.'
options: A) Managers should therefore avoid collecting data of any kind, since it cannot be of use to anyone.
B) Decisions are best left to those with the least information, who are least likely to be misled.
C) Information has become cheaper in recent decades, and so decisions are now better than in earlier times.
D) Beyond a point, however, additional information can degrade decisions rather than improve them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The blank must challenge the assumption in the first sentence, as the example of the hundred pages does. B and C overgeneralise; D contradicts the argument that cheaper information does not make decisions better.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Many people believe that a long queue means a good restaurant. ________ A diner who sees a crowd outside may infer that others know something she does not, and join it, which lengthens the queue and persuades the next passer-by. The queue may reflect nothing about the food.'
options: A) Restaurants with no queue are always better than those with one, since good food does not need to be waited for.
B) The belief can be self-reinforcing, since each person's choice is a signal to the next.
C) Queues exist because restaurants deliberately limit their seating in order to raise their prices over time.
D) Diners who join queues are usually familiar with the food, and so their judgement can be trusted entirely.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences that follow describe each diner's choice becoming a signal to the next. B, C and D introduce unrelated or contradictory claims.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The speaker's remarks, though ________ in tone, concealed a sharp criticism of the proposal.
options: A) belligerent
B) truculent
C) vitriolic
D) genial
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Genial' means friendly, which contrasts with the concealed sharp criticism. The other three are themselves hostile in tone.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

Having squandered the family fortune, he lived out his days in ________ circumstances.
options: A) opulent
B) straitened
C) affluent
D) magnificent
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Straitened' means limited by poverty. 'Opulent', 'affluent' and 'magnificent' all suggest wealth and splendour.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The proposal was criticised as a stopgap, since ________.
options: A) it had been drawn up over several years by a committee of independent experts in the field of study
B) it set out a permanent solution to the problem and a schedule for putting it into effect in full
C) it addressed the immediate shortage without touching the cause of it
D) it was approved by every department of the government without any amendment or objection at all
questions.explanation: Explanation: A stopgap is a temporary measure. Only the first option describes a measure that deals with symptoms rather than causes. B, C and D describe thoroughness or permanence.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

The memoir was ________ with errors, yet its author, ________ to correction, ________ every request for a revised edition.
options: A) riddled; impervious; declined
B) unblemished; impervious; declined
C) riddled; receptive; declined
D) riddled; impervious; solicited
questions.explanation: Explanation: A memoir 'riddled' with errors whose author is 'impervious' (closed) to correction would 'decline' a revised edition. 'Free' of errors contradicts 'yet'; 'receptive' and 'welcomed' contradict the author's refusal.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

Far from being ________ by the setback, the team grew more ________, and its ________ surprised even its critics.
options: A) emboldened; resolute; tenacity
B) disheartened; despondent; tenacity
C) disheartened; resolute; indifference
D) disheartened; resolute; tenacity
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Far from being disheartened' means the team was not discouraged, so it grew more 'resolute', and its 'tenacity' surprised critics. 'Despondent' and 'indifference' contradict this, and 'emboldened' does not fit 'far from being'.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) Her imminent departure from the firm was announced to the staff on Friday afternoon.
B) The eminent collapse of the bridge forced the road to be closed.
C) The new rules will affect small firms more than large ones, according to the report.
D) The report was commended for its candid assessment of the risks to the project.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Something about to happen is 'imminent'; 'eminent' means distinguished. 'Imminent', 'affect' (influence) and 'candid' are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The firm decided to adopt a new accounting standard from the start of the next financial year.
B) The prospective buyers inspected the house on Saturday morning before making an offer.
C) Visitors to the island must adapt the customs of its people.
D) The author's allusion to an earlier poem was lost on most of her readers at the time.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To take up customs is to 'adopt' them; 'adapt' means to adjust (and is followed by 'to'). 'Adopt', 'prospective' (likely to be) and 'allusion' (indirect reference) are used correctly.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'OBDURATE':
options: A) Acquiescent
B) Melancholy
C) Adamant
D) Gregarious
questions.explanation: Explanation: Obdurate means stubbornly refusing to change; 'adamant' is closest. 'Acquiescent' (compliant) is nearly the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'PARSIMONIOUS':
options: A) Frugal
B) Miserly
C) Thrifty
D) Lavish
questions.explanation: Explanation: Parsimonious means extremely unwilling to spend; 'lavish' is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'EPHEMERAL':
options: A) Transient
B) Interminable
C) Everlasting
D) Imperishable
questions.explanation: Explanation: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time; 'transient' is closest. The others mean lasting.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'GREGARIOUS':
options: A) Companionable
B) Reclusive
C) Outgoing
D) Convivial
questions.explanation: Explanation: Gregarious means fond of company; 'reclusive' (solitary) is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question:
Choose the correct meaning of the idiom:
'To cut corners' means to:
options: A) make a journey by the shortest route through the city, avoiding traffic delays on the way
B) reduce the number of employees in order to save money in a business that is in difficulty
C) attend to every small detail of a task before submitting it for approval to supervisors
D) do something cheaply or quickly, sacrificing quality
questions.explanation: Explanation: To cut corners is to save time or money by doing a job less thoroughly than it should be done.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which 'DISCRETE' is used correctly:
options: A) The detective made discrete enquiries among the neighbours so as not to alarm the people living nearby.
B) She was discrete about her plans, telling no one at the firm until the contract had been signed.
C) The study divided the participants into three discrete groups, with no overlap between them.
D) A discrete silence fell over the room as the speaker rose to address the members of the assembly.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Discrete' means separate and distinct. 'Discreet' (careful, tactful) is the word wanted in the other sentences.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

She is one of those writers who [is never satisfied] with a first draft.
options: A) has never been satisfied
B) are never satisfied
C) was never satisfied
D) being never satisfied
questions.explanation: Explanation: In 'one of those writers who...', 'who' refers to the plural 'writers', so the verb is plural: 'are'. The other options keep a singular verb, change the tense, or are not finite.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

The report criticises the firm [for failing to disclose the losses, for misleading investors, and its delay in] correcting the accounts.
options: A) for failing to disclose the losses, for misleading investors, and delaying
B) for its failure to disclose the losses, misleading investors, and its delay in
C) for failing to disclose the losses, misleading investors, and delaying
D) for failing to disclose the losses, to mislead investors, and delaying
questions.explanation: Explanation: The items after 'for' must be parallel gerunds: failing, misleading, delaying. The other options mix gerunds, infinitives and noun phrases or leave 'for' unevenly repeated.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The new policy has resulted in (A) / less complaints (B) / from customers than (C) / the old one did last year (D).'
options: A) The new policy has resulted in
B) less complaints
C) from customers than
D) the old one did last year
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Complaints' is countable, so the word needed is 'fewer'. The rest of the sentence is correct.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) Between you and me, the plan is unlikely to succeed.
B) Between you and I, the plan is unlikely to succeed at all.
C) Between you and myself, the plan is unlikely to succeed at all.
D) Between yourself and I, the plan is unlikely to succeed at all.
questions.explanation: Explanation: After a preposition the object pronoun 'me' is used: 'between you and me'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'The more he practised, ________ he became.'
options: A) more confident
B) the most confident
C) much more confident than
D) the more confident
questions.explanation: Explanation: The 'the more..., the more...' construction requires 'the' before the second comparative.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'She is allergic ________ penicillin.'
options: A) to
B) of
C) with
D) against
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Allergic' takes 'to'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Each of the students in the class has submitted a completed assignment.
B) Mathematics is the subject that most of the first-year students find hardest.
C) The news were welcomed across the country.
D) The scissors are on the table beside the window in the front room.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'News' is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'was welcomed'. The other sentences are correct.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'He insisted that she ________ the report before leaving.'
options: A) finish
B) finishes
C) finished
D) will finish
questions.explanation: Explanation: After verbs of insistence, recommendation or demand, the subjunctive (base form) is used: 'insisted that she finish'.
